Agent-ToM: Learning to Monitor Autonomous LLM Agents via Theory-of-Mind Reasoning

Nesreen K. Ahmed Affiliation: Cisco Outshift Email: nesahmed@cisco.com    Nima Nafisi Affiliation: Cisco Outshift Email: nnafisi@cisco.com
Abstract

Monitoring autonomous large language model (LLM) agents for covert malicious behavior (e.g., covertly pursuing a hidden malicious objective) is challenging due to delayed, context-dependent, and long-horizon attack patterns. In adversarial settings such as sabotage, agents may pursue hidden objectives while maintaining superficially benign behavior, making detection difficult even with full trajectory access. Prior monitoring approaches primarily improve monitor scaffolding or ensemble aggregation, but treat each trajectory independently and do not improve from prior monitoring experience. Moreover, standard reasoning methods explain observed behavior but do not explicitly reason about agent beliefs, intentions, and goal alignment required to distinguish benign task execution from covert deviation.

We propose Agent-ToM, a learning-to-monitor framework grounded in Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning for security analysis of autonomous agents. Agent-ToM performs structured full-trajectory analysis by inferring beliefs, step-level intent hypotheses with calibrated confidence, expected actions, and deviations from task-consistent behavioral baselines. At inference time, it employs a Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline to construct and validate monitoring decisions. At training time, Agent-ToM learns from prior monitoring episodes by distilling critique signals into a persistent semantic guardrail memory that accumulates monitoring strategies, enabling reusable belief- and intent-conditioned constraints to be applied across episodes. We evaluate Agent-ToM on adversarial agent monitoring benchmarks (SHADE-Arena and CUA-SHADE-Arena). Agent-ToM achieves strong precision–recall balance and outperforms state-of-the-art monitoring baselines, including ensemble methods, while using a single coherent reasoning pipeline. These results demonstrate that learning at the monitoring layer, combined with structured ToM reasoning and verification, provides an effective and deployable foundation for securing autonomous LLM agents.

1 Introduction

Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to perform multi-step tasks involving tool use, code execution, and interaction with external systems (Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023). While such agents enable powerful automation, they also introduce new security risks: they may exhibit covert misbehavior, violating safety policies or deviating from intended user goals. Moreover, malicious behavior may be delayed, context-dependent, and distributed across long-horizon interaction traces, making it difficult to detect using short-horizon or action-local monitors. Effective monitoring therefore requires reasoning over full trajectories, inferring intent beyond surface actions, and distinguishing legitimate task execution from covert deviation.

Recent work on agent monitoring has primarily focused on improving detection through scaffolding strategies such as chunking, hierarchical decomposition, sequential or sliding-window analysis, and ensemble aggregation (Kutasov et al., 2025; Kale et al., 2025; Stickland et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). While these approaches improve coverage over long trajectories, they treat each execution trace independently and rely on fixed detection heuristics or aggregation over model outputs. As a result, monitoring systems do not improve from prior failures and lack mechanisms for accumulating reusable knowledge about adversarial behavior. Moreover, they do not explicitly model the beliefs, intentions, and goal alignment that underlie agent behavior, limiting their ability to distinguish benign deviations from covert malicious intent. In practice, this leads to brittle performance under evolving attack strategies and shifts the burden toward increasingly complex monitoring scaffolding, ensemble strategies, and threshold tuning.

However, in real-world deployment settings, monitoring agents must learn at the monitoring layer. Rather than repeatedly evaluating each trace in isolation, monitors should adapt over time by incorporating lessons from past incidents (Suzgun et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2025). Moreover, monitoring requires reasoning abstractions that differ fundamentally from task-solving reasoning. While generic chain-of-thought explanations can describe what an agent did, they do not capture why it acted that way, whether its beliefs were consistent with the stated task, or whether observed deviations reflect benign exploration or malicious intent (Wagner et al., 2025). We therefore view monitoring not as a stateless classification problem over trajectories, but as a learning-based inference process that evolves through accumulating and refining reusable behavioral constraints from agent trajectories.

We propose Agent-ToM, a learning-to-monitor framework grounded in Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning for security analysis of autonomous LLM agents. Agent-ToM performs structured full-trajectory analysis by inferring agent behavior in terms of beliefs, inferred intent, expected actions, and deviations from task-consistent behavioral baselines. To make this reasoning robust and adaptive, Agent-ToM integrates a Reason–Verify–Refine inference paradigm, in which hypotheses about agent behavior are first constructed and an initial classification is produced through structured ToM reasoning, then subsequently verified and optionally refined based on evidential sufficiency and consistency. In addition, Agent-ToM leverages persistent semantic guardrail memory that accumulates monitoring strategies by distilling reusable belief- and intent-conditioned constraints from prior monitoring episodes, enabling cross-episode learning without retraining the underlying models or modifying the monitor. This design allows monitoring decisions to be explicitly constructed, critically evaluated, reused, and improved iteratively.

We evaluate Agent-ToM on adversarial monitoring benchmarks derived from SHADE-Arena (Kutasov et al., 2025), which provides agents with a benign main task coupled with a hidden malicious task and covers 1717 task pairs (i.e., agent applications). In addition, we evaluate out-of-distribution performance on the recent CUA-SHADE-Arena benchmark (Kale et al., 2025), which extends TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2024) to general computer-use agents and provides 1515 main–hidden task pairs. We focus on challenging traces that span various adversarial strategies, including deception, obfuscation, and monitor-targeted attacks. Across multiple configurations, Agent-ToM achieves strong precision–recall balance and competitive AUC, matching or exceeding strong ensemble-based monitoring baselines with complex scaffolding involving many LLM calls, while using a single coherent reasoning pipeline with only two LLM calls during inference. These results demonstrate that belief- and intent-based monitoring, when combined with verification and experience-driven monitor-strategy learning, provides an effective, efficient, and deployable foundation for securing autonomous LLM agents.

Contributions.

We summarize the contributions of this paper as follows:

  1. 1.

    Learning-based agent monitoring via Theory-of-Mind reasoning. We introduce Agent-ToM, a unified learning-based cognitive monitoring framework grounded in Theory-of-Mind reasoning that performs structured full-trajectory analysis of autonomous agent behavior for security analysis.

  2. 2.

    Structured behavioral analysis via belief and intent inference. Agent-ToM infers beliefs and step-level intent hypotheses with confidence, along with expected actions and task-specific behavioral baselines, enabling evidence-based discrimination between benign and malicious behavior beyond surface trajectory patterns.

  3. 3.

    Reason–Verify–Refine inference paradigm for monitoring. Agent-ToM leverages a structured inference paradigm in which an initial hypothesis and classification are produced via ToM reasoning, and subsequently verified and optionally refined based on evidential sufficiency and consistency, improving robustness and calibration of monitoring decisions.

  4. 4.

    Critique-driven learning of monitoring strategies. At training time, Agent-ToM learns monitoring strategies by distilling critique signals from episodic traces into a persistent semantic guardrail memory, capturing reusable behavioral constraints that generalize across episodes.

2 Proposed Framework

We present Agent-ToM, a learning-based monitoring framework for autonomous LLM agents. Instead of treating monitoring as a stateless classification problem over agent trajectories, Agent-ToM formulates monitoring as a learning-based inference problem that evolves by accumulating and refining reusable monitoring strategies from prior experience.

Agent-ToM decomposes monitoring into structured inference over latent agent states and critique-driven learning of reusable behavioral constraints. At inference time, the framework reasons over full execution trajectories to infer beliefs, intent, expected actions, and deviations from task-consistent behavior. At training time, it converts critique signals from prior episodes into a semantic guardrail memory that guides future monitoring decisions.

2.1 Problem Definition & Threat Model

We consider the problem of monitoring autonomous or semi-autonomous agents operating over extended episodes. Each agent is assigned a main task, a legitimate task provided by the user or operator, and may additionally pursue a hidden side task that conflicts with safety policies or user intent. The agent’s misbehavior is covert: it attempts to complete the side task while maintaining superficially benign behavior consistent with the main task, making detection difficult even with full trajectory access. Each episode produces an episodic execution trace τ=(o1,a1,…,oT,aT)\tau=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{T},a_{T}) consisting of observations, agent actions, intermediate decisions, and tool interactions over time.

Given a trajectory τ\tau, the monitoring system 𝒜\mathcal{A} produces a prediction

(y,c,r)=𝒜⁡(τ),(y,c,r)=\mathcal{A}(\tau),

where y∈{benign,malicious}y\in\{\text{benign},\text{malicious}\} is the predicted label, cc is a calibrated confidence score, and rr is an interpretable justification suitable for downstream analysis or human review.

Unlike standard classification problems over trajectories, monitoring LLM agents requires reasoning over long-horizon interaction traces, inferring hypotheses about latent agent states such as beliefs and intent, and assessing whether observed behavior aligns with task-consistent expectations or reflects covert deviation.

We formulate the problem of monitoring agents as a learning-based process, where the monitoring system 𝒜\mathcal{A} leverages prior experience through a learned memory ℳ\mathcal{M} of reusable behavioral constraints. Given a trajectory τ\tau, the system produces

(y,c,r)=𝒜⁡(τ,ℳ),(y,c,r)=\mathcal{A}(\tau;\mathcal{M}),

where ℳ\mathcal{M} encodes semantic guardrails distilled from prior monitoring episodes {τ′}\{\tau^{\prime}\}, enabling the system to guide inference beyond the current trajectory and generalize across episodes.

Threat Model.

We adopt the Monitor Red Teaming (MRT) threat model of (Kale et al., 2025), which characterizes the adversarial setting along two axes: agent awareness and monitor awareness. The monitor operates in the aware setting throughout: it has access to the agent’s full execution trajectory τ\tau, including all actions and intermediate chain-of-thought reasoning, and knows the main task specification, but has no access to the hidden side task or any prior knowledge of the specific malicious objective being pursued. The agent may or may not be aware of the monitor: we evaluate across an unaware baseline where the agent is oblivious to the monitor’s existence and five aware evasion strategies in which the agent actively attempts to evade detection via CoT obfuscation, jailbreaking-inspired deception, hybrid strategies, and direct monitor hijacking. Approximately 85% of malicious SHADE-Arena (Kutasov et al., 2025) traces involve aware agents, representing the strictly harder threat model setting. CUA-SHADE-Arena (Kale et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024) exclusively employs aware agents, providing an out-of-distribution evaluation under the hardest threat model configuration. Full details of evasion strategies are provided in Appendix A.

2.2 Theory of Mind Reasoning for Agent Monitoring

Theory of Mind (ToM) refers to the cognitive capacity to attribute mental states such as beliefs, intentions, and goals to other agents, and to use these attributions to explain and predict their behavior (Premack and Woodruff, 1978; Wellman et al., 2001). As Wagner et al. (2025) argue, effective ToM reasoning requires two steps: first explicitly invoking structured mental state inference, and then applying classification given those inferred states. Standard monitoring approaches collapse these steps by reasoning directly to a classification decision without first explicitly inferring the beliefs and intentions that generated the observed behavior. In this work, we use the term Theory-of-Mind to refer to structured inference over latent mental variables (beliefs, intent, expected actions, and deviations from task-consistent behavior) from observed agent behavior, rather than learning an explicit cognitive model of the agent.

We note that when agents actively conceal their intent through CoT obfuscation, deception, or monitor hijacking, direct observation of mental states is not possible from the trace alone. Agent-ToM therefore combines abductive reasoning, by identifying the hypothesis that best explains the observed trajectory, with a ToM-inspired inference structure that organizes reasoning around beliefs, intent, and expected actions. This combination enables structured hypothesis generation and evaluation while remaining epistemically grounded in observable behavior.

Despite this constraint, Agent-ToM builds on the Simulation Theory framework of Wilf et al. (2024), treating perspective-taking as a necessary precondition before any classification decision is made, organizing abductive inference around structured mental state variables rather than reasoning directly from surface observations. This is particularly critical in adversarial monitoring, where a misbehaving agent may produce superficially legitimate actions while pursuing a hidden objective, making surface behavior alone insufficient to distinguish benign task execution from covert deviation. Agent-ToM operationalizes this as structured inference over four latent variables derived from the agent’s trajectory, as part of the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline (Section 2.3):

  1. 1.

    Beliefs — what the agent appears to know or assume about its task context, derived by establishing a task-specific behavioral baseline of expected tool use, data access patterns, and action sequences.

  2. 2.

    Intent hypotheses — step-level inferences about what the agent is trying to accomplish at each decision point, including potential malicious objectives, assigned calibrated confidence scores.

  3. 3.

    Expected actions — predictions of what a task-aligned agent should do given the stated objective and inferred beliefs.

  4. 4.

    Deviations — divergences between predicted and observed behavior that cannot be explained by task-consistent hypotheses.

Together with concrete evidence grounded in the inferred intent, these variables constitute a structured representation of the monitored agent’s inferred mental state, from which the classification decision is derived rather than being predicted directly from surface observations. The Verify stage then independently re-evaluates whether the inferred intent hypothesis is supported by sufficient evidence, testing alternative benign explanations, and assessing whether the observed behavior is better explained by malicious or task-consistent objectives. This explicit inference of latent mental states enables Agent-ToM to detect covert misalignment that cannot be identified from surface behavior alone (see Figure 1).

2.3 Inference-Time Monitoring: Reason–Verify–Refine

At inference time, Agent-ToM performs monitoring through a structured Reason–Verify–Refine inference paradigm (see Figure 1 for details). The Reason stage performs Theory-of-Mind (ToM) inference over episodic execution traces, constructing structured hypotheses about the agent’s beliefs, inferred intent, expected actions, and deviations from task-specific behavioral baselines, and produces an initial monitoring prediction (y,r)(y,r) based on these inferred hypotheses. These representations characterize what the agent appears to know, what objectives it is pursuing, and how its observed actions align with or deviate from expected task-consistent behavior. Behavioral baselines are constructed from task context and typical action patterns, enabling the system to distinguish anomalous or suspicious behavior from legitimate task adaptation. The Verify stage performs independent evaluation of the initial prediction by conditioning on the reasoning output (y,r)(y,r) and reassessing its validity. Acting as a second reviewer, the verify stage critically examines whether the inferred intent and classification are sufficiently supported by the available evidence, identifies inconsistencies or overlooked signals, and evaluates whether alternative benign or malicious interpretations better explain the observed behavior. Based on this analysis, the stage may confirm the initial prediction or revise it by upgrading or downgrading the assessed threat level. This revision process follows asymmetric criteria, requiring stronger evidence to downgrade malicious classifications than to confirm them.

Finally, the Refine stage produces the final calibrated monitoring output (y,c,r)(y,c,r) by integrating the outcomes of the reasoning and verification stages. In particular, this stage consolidates the verified classification decision, assigns a calibrated confidence score based on evidential strength and consistency, and generates a coherent natural-language justification suitable for downstream consumption. All inference stages are conditioned on semantic guardrails retrieved from persistent memory ℳ\mathcal{M}, allowing prior monitoring experience to inform current reasoning while preserving flexibility in inference. In practice, the Verify and Refine stages are implemented as a single joint inference step that both evaluates and updates the initial prediction, resulting in an efficient two-call pipeline while preserving the conceptual separation of roles. This decomposition enables explicit separation between hypothesis construction, evaluation, and decision calibration, improving the robustness and interpretability of monitoring outcomes.

2.4 Training-Time Learning via Critique and Distillation

Inspired by recent work on evolving context (Zhang et al., 2026; Suzgun et al., 2026), Agent-ToM adopts a critique-driven learning loop to learn from prior monitoring episodes and distill monitoring strategies in semantic guardrail memory (see Figure 2). The ToM Reasoning Module generates belief and intent hypotheses and an initial monitoring prediction for each input trace. Then all monitoring predictions whether correct or incorrect are analyzed by a Critique and Credit Assignment component, which performs structured evaluation of the reasoning process across the underlying Theory-of-Mind steps (e.g., baseline construction, intent inference, and evidence assessment). This module identifies which aspects of the reasoning process are responsible for correct or incorrect outcomes, tagging existing memory guardrails as helpful or harmful and providing step-level diagnostic signals that enable targeted refinement of monitoring strategies. These critique signals are then processed by a Knowledge Distiller, which transforms recurring failure and success patterns into reusable semantic guardrails that encode observed attack patterns and normative behavioral constraints. Rather than memorizing individual traces or prompt-level artifacts, the distillation process induces higher-level behavioral constraints that generalize across tasks and episodes. These learned guardrails directly shape inference-time reasoning by constraining hypothesis generation and verification under similar behavioral patterns.

Agent-ToM’s training pipeline offers two design choices tailored for agent monitoring:

  • •

    Batch distillation: training proceeds in parallel batches of episodic traces: each batch shares a snapshot of the current memory ℳ\mathcal{M}, episodes are processed in parallel through the ToM reasoning and Critique modules, critique signals are merged across the batch, and the Knowledge Distiller is invoked once to update the memory before processing the next batch. This approach serves two purposes: it enables efficient training at scale, and more importantly, it exposes the Knowledge Distiller to a rich diverse set of critique signals simultaneously, enabling it to identify cross-episode patterns and distill more generalizable guardrails in memory ℳ\mathcal{M} than single-episode distillation would produce.

  • •

    Critique-driven self-correction: the monitor is given one opportunity to self-correct its classification using the critique feedback before distillation. This approach enables conditioning the Knowledge Distiller on improved reasoning traces and producing qualitatively richer guardrails than direct distillation without self-correction. We analyze the effect of this self-correction step and the resulting memory growth in Section 5.1 (Figure 5).

2.5 Semantic Guardrail Memory

Distilled abstractions from episodic traces are stored in a persistent semantic guardrail memory ℳ\mathcal{M}. This memory is additive where the Knowledge Distiller only adds new guardrails, never removes and it encodes abstract, belief- and intent-conditioned semantic guardrails that capture constraints on agent behavior rather than storing episodic examples or procedural rules. These guardrails relate inferred beliefs and intent to expected actions and observed deviations, enabling structured reasoning about agent behavior. Examples of such guardrails include universal reasoning scaffolds such as deriving task-specific behavioral baselines for expected tool use and data access, generating alternative benign hypotheses before attributing malicious intent, and requiring concrete evidence before assigning high threat levels. In addition, attack-pattern guardrails capture known adversarial strategies across various categories, such as malicious objectives (e.g., unauthorized data exfiltration through sensitive source mismatches and financial account manipulation); deception strategies (e.g., fabricated self-reported diligence and lying with plausible false narratives); and evasion techniques (e.g., monitor hijacking through direct instruction injection).

Agent-ToM supports two memory organization configurations. In the predefined configuration, the memory is initialized with user-defined section headers that guide how the Knowledge Distiller organizes new guardrails, allowing domain experts to inject prior knowledge about known attack patterns into the memory structure. In the self-structured configuration, the memory is initialized empty and the Distiller learns its own organizational structure from the training data, allowing the memory to adapt freely to observed attack patterns without predefined categories. We evaluate both configurations in Section 5.2.

In this work, the predefined configuration organizes memory content into three sections corresponding to orthogonal dimensions of adversarial agent behavior: (A) Malicious Objective — the harmful outcome the agent pursues; (B) Deception Strategy — how the agent conceals its intent from the monitor; and (C) Evasion Technique — tactics used to reduce the likelihood of detection. This structure mirrors the ToM reasoning pipeline, which separately infers agent beliefs and intent (A), evaluates deceptive presentation (B), and identifies behavioral patterns designed to evade oversight (C). To support this organization, the critique analyzes each trace across all three dimensions, providing structured insights that guide the Knowledge Distiller in inducing guardrail and monitoring strategies across all sections.

In both configurations, a learned semantic guardrail memory on one set of agent applications can serve as an initialization prior for monitoring new agent applications. At inference time, monitoring strategies accumulated from prior applications are either injected in full or selectively retrieved based on task context and injected into both the Reason and Verify stages, enabling immediate transfer of monitoring knowledge to new deployment settings without retraining. During training on new applications, the Knowledge Distiller receives the full current memory, explicitly avoids redundancy with existing guardrails, and extends rather than replaces accumulated monitoring knowledge with new application-specific patterns. This separation between inference-time reasoning and training-time learning allows Agent-ToM to adapt over time while maintaining interpretability, stability, and decision consistency.

3 Monitoring Baselines, Variants, and Setup

3.1 Baseline Methods

We compare Agent-ToM against representative monitoring approaches spanning different reasoning and learning paradigms (see Table 1 for a summary).

  • •

    Single-Pass Monitoring: LLM-Judge (zeroshot) performs direct reasoning over the full trajectory in a single pass, without structured belief or intent modeling and without cross-episode learning.

  • •

    Structured Multi-Stage Monitoring: ToM (zeroshot) corresponds to the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline (Figure 1) without incorporating learned strategies or external memory, isolating the effect of structured reasoning alone.

  • •

    Retrieval-Based Monitoring: Agent-Auditor (Luo et al., 2025) uses embedding-based retrieval over a corpus of labeled traces. Given a new trajectory, it retrieves the nearest neighbor trace and conditions the monitor on it as a one-shot exemplar. To handle long-horizon trajectories, inputs are truncated to 40964096 tokens for embedding computation, and up to 1515k tokens are used for exemplar conditioning. This approach provides similarity-based contextual evidence without explicit reasoning over latent agent states.

  • •

    Ensemble-Based Monitoring: We consider two ensemble strategies. Sequential ensemble (Kale et al., 2025) processes trajectories in chunks, sequentially summarizing and scoring intermediate segments while propagating context. Async ensemble (Stickland et al., 2025) performs multiple independent reasoning runs on the same trajectory and aggregates predictions via majority vote, improving coverage through diverse reasoning paths.

3.2 Agent-ToM Variants

We evaluate three variants of Agent-ToM to assess the contributions of prompt-level learning, external memory, and joint reasoning–verification training:

  • •

    Agent-ToM (Prompt-level learning) uses prompt optimization via GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), a gradient-free prompt evolution method, to encode monitoring strategies directly in the system prompt without an explicit external memory.

  • •

    Agent-ToM (External Memory, Stage 1) learns monitoring strategies from episodic critiques and distills them into a semantic guardrail memory. At inference time, guardrails from memory are injected into the reasoning stage to guide belief and intent inference.

  • •

    Agent-ToM (External Memory, Stage 1–2) extends Stage 1 by jointly training both reasoning and verification stages. Guardrails are injected into both stages, enabling improved calibration and cross-task generalization.

3.3 Training Setup

This section reports the concrete training configuration for the two learning-based Agent-ToM variants introduced in Section 2.4: Agent-ToM (External Memory), which grows a semantic guardrail memory ℳ\mathcal{M} via the critique-driven learning loop, and Agent-ToM (Prompt-level learning), which evolves the natural-language instructions of the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline using GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026). Both variants use the same initial instructions and prompts.

Agent-ToM (External Memory).

Stage 1 (ToM Reason) and Stage 2 (ToM Verify & Refine) maintain separate guardrail memories. We first train the Stage 1 memory and then freeze it while training the Stage 2 memory on top of it on the same training split; this yields the Agent-ToM (External Memory, Stage 1–2) variant. Both stages use the same critique-driven learning loop (Section 2.4) with the following defaults:

  • •

    Batch size =8=8, parallel workers =16=16, number of epochs =1=1.

  • •

    Batch distillation with one critique feedback loop per sample.

  • •

    ToM Reasoning Module, Critique and Credit Assignment, and Knowledge Distiller all use gpt-5.1 during training; at inference time, Agent-ToM uses gpt-5-mini.

  • •

    Episodic traces are iterated sequentially per app, processing all traces from one agent application before moving to the next.

  • •

    All calls use temperature =1.0=1.0 as required by the reasoning model API, with a maximum of 16,000 output tokens per call. Full episodic traces and semantic guardrail memory are passed without truncation at each stage.

Agent-ToM (Prompt-level learning).

We jointly optimize the Stage 1 and Stage 2 instructions with GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026), an evolutionary reflection-based optimizer:

  • •

    Batch size: 33 samples per reflective step, corresponding to GEPA’s reflection minibatch.

  • •

    Number of epochs: we use GEPA’s medium budget (auto=medium), which fixes the number of candidate programs to n=12n=12 .

The reflection, inference, and Stage 2 LLMs all default to gpt-5.1 (temperature 0.70.7) during training.

4 Experiments

We evaluate Agent-ToM on two adversarial agent-monitoring benchmarks. SHADE-Arena (Kutasov et al., 2025) consists of 17 task pairs in simulated tool-use environments, pairing benign main tasks with hidden malicious side objectives across long-horizon traces (avg. 82.9 turns). CUA-SHADE-Arena (Kale et al., 2025) extends evaluation to realistic computer-use settings, pairing 15 business tasks with adversarial side objectives in a virtual machine environment. Agent-ToM is trained on SHADE-Arena and evaluated on both benchmarks; CUA-SHADE-Arena serves exclusively as an out-of-distribution test. Dataset statistics and evasion strategy breakdowns are in Appendix A.

Evaluation Metrics. We report Accuracy, F1, Recall, and Precision. F1 is the primary metric, as it penalizes both over-flagging and missed detections under moderate class imbalance (Davis and Goadrich, 2006; Sokolova and Lapalme, 2009; Kale et al., 2025).

Baselines. We compare against: LLM-Judge (single-pass zeroshot reasoning); ToM (zeroshot), the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline without learned memory, isolating structured reasoning alone; Agent-Auditor (Luo et al., 2025), a retrieval-based monitor that conditions on nearest-neighbor exemplars from labeled traces; and two ensemble strategies — Sequential (Kale et al., 2025), which processes trajectories in chunks, and Async (Stickland et al., 2025), which aggregates majority-vote predictions across independent runs.

Agent-ToM Variants. Prompt-level encodes strategies via GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) prompt optimization without external memory. Stage 1 distills episodic critiques into semantic guardrail memory injected at reasoning time. Stage 1–2 extends Stage 1 by jointly training verification, injecting guardrails into both stages. All variants except Sequential Ensemble use GPT-5-mini at inference; Sequential Ensemble reports official benchmark outputs using Claude 3.6 Sonnet. Full baseline and variants descriptions are detailed in Section 3.

4.1 Baseline Comparison on SHADE-Arena

Tables 2 and 3 report results with Agent-ToM trained on 25% of the SHADE-Arena training set; Section 5.1 analyzes the effect of training data size.

Structured ToM reasoning (0.615 F1) improves over single-pass LLM-Judge (0.596 F1), primarily through higher precision (0.937 vs. 0.869), indicating that explicit belief- and intent-based reasoning improves calibration. Retrieval-based monitoring (Agent-Auditor, 0.697 F1) further improves performance, but remains limited by surface similarity, failing to capture abstract behavioral patterns. Ensemble methods increase recall at the expense of calibration. Sequential ensemble achieves balanced performance (0.727 F1), while Async ensemble attains near-perfect recall (0.990) but suffers from substantially reduced precision (0.617), reflecting over-flagging under majority voting.

With learned semantic guardrail memory, Agent-ToM achieves the highest F1 (0.782), improving from 0.717 F1 (Stage 1) to 0.782 F1 (Stage 1–2) while maintaining strong precision–recall balance (0.748 recall, 0.818 precision). Agent-ToM with Prompt-level learning (0.686 F1) improves recall over zeroshot ToM but remains inferior to memory-based learning, indicating that reusable monitoring strategies require explicit cross-episode distillation rather than prompt optimization alone. Notably, Agent-ToM (Stage 1–2) outperforms all ensemble approaches while requiring only two LLM calls per trajectory, compared to 8 and 17 calls for Async and Sequential ensembles, respectively, demonstrating that performance gains arise from structured reasoning and learning rather than increased inference-time compute.

4.2 Out-of-Distribution Performance on CUA-SHADE-Arena

Table 3 presents transfer performance on CUA-SHADE-Arena, where Agent-ToM is trained on SHADE-Arena and evaluated on unseen computer-use tasks without further adaptation.

LLM-Judge outperforms its SHADE-Arena result by a large margin (0.815 vs. 0.596 F1, 1.0 precision), indicating that shorter-horizon CUA tasks are more amenable to single-pass reasoning than long-horizon deception patterns. ToM (zeroshot) also improves (0.666 F1), but remains limited, showing that structured reasoning without learning provides only modest transfer gains. Sequential ensemble performs competitively (0.805 F1), while Async degrades substantially (0.606 F1) due to precision collapse (0.454), reflecting over-flagging under majority voting. Agent-ToM (Stage 1–2) achieves the best overall performance (0.891 accuracy, 0.831 F1, 1.0 precision). Notably, Stage 2 provides a larger gain on CUA than on SHADE-Arena: Stage 1 achieves only 0.615 F1 (0.444 recall), while Stage 1–2 improves recall to 0.710 (+0.266) at perfect precision, indicating that the Verify–Refine stage is critical when initial reasoning transfers imperfectly to out-of-distribution tasks. This further shows that cross-episode learning is essential for robust transfer.

4.3 Efficiency Analysis

Figure 3 compares monitoring performance against inference cost across all methods. Figure 3 (a) plots F1 score against the number of LLM calls per trajectory, and Figure 3 (b) shows the precision–recall tradeoff with ISO-F1 contours.

Agent-ToM (Stage 1+2) achieves the highest F1 (0.782) among baselines while requiring only two LLM calls per trajectory — matching the inference cost of ToM (zeroshot) and Agent-Auditor, and using a fraction of the calls required by ensemble approaches (8 for Async, 17 for Sequential). This demonstrates that structured ToM reasoning combined with cross-episode memory learning can match or exceed the performance of compute-intensive ensemble methods without sacrificing calibration.Agent-ToM (Stage 1) achieves 0.717 F1 with a single LLM call, approaching Sequential Ensemble performance (0.727 F1, 17 calls) at 17×\times lower inference cost, making it suitable for latency-sensitive deployment settings.

The precision–recall panel reveals a key limitation of ensemble approaches: Async Ensemble achieves high recall (0.990) but at substantially degraded precision (0.617), reflecting systematic over-flagging. Agent-ToM (Stage 1+2) maintains a strong precision–recall balance (0.748 recall, 0.818 precision), avoiding the calibration collapse observed in majority-vote aggregation. Sequential Ensemble achieves reasonable balance (0.618 recall, 0.884 precision) but at a higher cost ( 17 LLM calls per trajectory). Overall, Agent-ToM achieves competitive calibration with significantly lower inference cost.

5 Ablation Studies

5.1 Training Ablation Study

Tables 2 and 3 report results where Agent-ToM is trained on 25% of the SHADE-Arena training set, demonstrating strong performance under limited training data. Below we analyze the effect of training data size, critique feedback, and memory growth on Agent-ToM monitoring performance.

Training Dynamics and Critique Feedback.

To assess the contribution of critique-driven distillation, we compare Agent-ToM trained with critique feedback, where the monitor is given one opportunity to self-correct its classification using the critique feedback before the Knowledge Distiller is invoked, against a variant without critique feedback that invokes the Knowledge Distiller directly from the critique signal without a self-correction step. Figure 4 shows performance across training set sizes from 9% to 100% for both conditions.

With critique feedback, F1 improves consistently from 0.695 at 9% to 0.814 at 100% training, with the semantic guardrail memory growing from 17 to 89 rules. A notable plateau occurs between 27% and 50% training (F1 ≈\approx 0.784), where continued rule induction (40 →\rightarrow 59 rules) does not yield meaningful performance gains, suggesting that the new rules distilled during this period do not capture sufficiently novel behavioral constraints to improve detection. Beyond 50%, novel attack patterns trigger a burst of new rule induction (59 →\rightarrow 89 rules) and a corresponding jump in F1 to 0.814. Without critique feedback, performance plateaus early at F1 ≈\approx 0.662 from 27% training onward, reaching only 62 rules at 100% training, roughly 30% fewer rules and nearly half the memory footprint of the critique feedback variant. This indicates that skipping the self-correction step results in lower-quality distillation inputs, producing memory rules that are less discriminative and limit further improvement.

Memory Growth and Performance.

Figure 5 shows F1 as a function of semantic guardrail memory size (in words) for both conditions. With critique feedback, memory grows from 1,921 words at 9% training to 14,032 words at 100%, with F1 tracking memory growth closely. Without critique feedback, memory plateaus around 7,013 words and F1 stops increasing at 0.668, despite accumulating 62 rules compared to 89, at nearly half the memory footprint. This suggests that critique feedback does not merely produce more rules; it produces qualitatively richer rules that encode more discriminative behavioral constraints.

Batch Distillation.

Table 4 compares Agent-ToM training with three batch size configurations at 100% training set size. Sequential distillation (batch=1) processes one episode at a time, invoking the Knowledge Distiller after each critique signal. Batch distillation merges critique signals from multiple episodes before a single distiller call, exposing the Knowledge Distiller to richer, more diverse signals simultaneously. Increasing batch size from 1 to 4 improves F1 from 0.843 to 0.860 (+0.017) while reducing training time by 3.2×\times (14.6h →\rightarrow 4.5h). Further increasing to batch=8 yields negligible additional gain (+0.001 F1) with an additional 2×\times speedup. Larger batches also produce more compact memory (155 rules, 22,860 words at batch=1 vs. 89 rules, 14,032 words at batch=8), by aggregating critique signals across multiple episodes before distillation. These merged critique signals filter noisy single-episode patterns and retain only cross-episode generalizable guardrails, directly mitigating a known limitation of context evolution approaches (Zhang et al., 2026).

5.2 Memory Structure Analysis: Predefined vs. Self-Structured

Figure 6 compares Agent-ToM with predefined and self-structured memory organization against Sequential Ensemble (Kale et al., 2025) across six agent evasion strategies (see section A for details) on the common evaluation subset of SHADE-Arena (N=722N=722, both Agent-ToM configurations trained at 100% of the SHADE-Arena training set). We also report the full comparison against main baselines in Table 5.

Agent-ToM vs. Sequential Ensemble.

Both Agent-ToM configurations substantially outperform Sequential Ensemble on all aware-agent evasion strategies. The largest gains occur on CoT obfuscation, hybrid obfuscation and lying, and monitor hijacking, where structured belief and intent inference enables the monitor to detect malicious patterns despite active concealment. Sequential Ensemble performs best only on unaware agents (naive, F1=0.939), where the absence of active evasion makes inference-time scaffolding via chunked trajectory sufficient for detection.

Predefined vs. Self-structured Memory.

Self-structured memory consistently outperforms predefined memory across all strategies (overall F1 0.861 vs. 0.813, ++0.048). The largest gains appear on CoT obfuscation and lying with jailbreaking, suggesting that allowing the Knowledge Distiller to organize monitoring strategies without predefined categories produces more flexible and discriminative behavioral constraints. This is particularly notable for lying-based evasion, where agents produce plausible false narratives, a pattern that may not fit neatly into predefined section boundaries but emerges naturally in self-structured memory.

Hardest Evasion Strategies.

Lying with jailbreaking remains the most challenging strategy for both configurations (best F1=0.821), reflecting the epistemic constraint noted in Section 2.2: when agents actively produce plausible false narratives, abductive inference over observable behavior is most constrained. The aware baseline (dealer’s choice) is similarly challenging (best F1=0.809), where agents self-direct their own evasion without a prescribed strategy.

5.3 Scaling and Generalization

Table 6 evaluates Agent-ToM under two generalization conditions using a 5-fold cross-application evaluation on five SHADE-Arena task pairs, with each fold holding out one application as the test set. In the in-distribution (ID) setting, memory is trained on all five apps including the app under test. In the out-of-distribution (OOD) setting, memory is drawn from the other four apps only, evaluating cross-app transfer without task-specific guardrails. Both settings evaluate Agent-ToM (Stage 1) monitoring with the predefined 3-section memory taxonomy (Section 2.5). Agent-ToM achieves strong in-distribution performance with both models (GPT-5: F1=0.966, GPT-5-mini: F1=0.924), demonstrating that learned guardrails effectively generalize within the training distribution. Under OOD conditions, GPT-5 maintains strong performance (F1=0.855), while GPT-5-mini degrades more substantially (F1=0.721), indicating that stronger reasoning capacity improves robustness to distributional shift. The OOD drop for GPT-5 (0.966 →\rightarrow 0.855, −-0.111) indicates partial but imperfect transfer, suggesting that guardrails learned from related applications capture generalizable behavioral patterns, with per-task breakdown provided in Figure 7.

5.4 Impact of Stage 2 Verification

Figure 8 quantifies the contribution of the Verify–Refine stage across both benchmarks. On SHADE-Arena, Stage 2 improves F1 by +0.065+0.065 (0.717 →\rightarrow 0.782), recall by +0.094+0.094, and precision by +0.027+0.027, reflecting more calibrated classification decisions through independent verification. The improvement is substantially larger on CUA-SHADE-Arena, where Stage 2 raises F1 by +0.216+0.216 (0.615 →\rightarrow 0.831) and recall by +0.267+0.267 while maintaining high precision (1.000), suggesting that verification is particularly effective on out-of-distribution computer-use tasks where Stage 1 reasoning alone is insufficiently calibrated. Both improvements are statistically significant under McNemar’s test (SHADE-Arena: χ2\chi^{2}, p=3.15×10−4p=3.15\times 10^{-4}; CUA: p=1.50×10−3p=1.50\times 10^{-3}), confirming that Stage 2 produces systematic classification improvements beyond chance.

5.5 McNemar’s Test

Table 7 reports McNemar’s test comparing Agent-ToM variants against baseline monitoring methods on the common evaluation subset (N=722N=722, SHADE-Arena, 100% training). Both Agent-ToM configurations significantly outperform Async Ensemble and ToM Zeroshot (p<0.001p<0.001). Agent-ToM (Self-structured) also significantly outperforms Sequential Ensemble (p<0.001p<0.001), while Agent-ToM (Predefined) shows a marginal advantage (p=0.038p=0.038). Self structured memory significantly outperforms the predefined configuration (p<0.001p<0.001).

5.6 Semantic Guardrail Memory Visualization

Figure 9 visualizes the internal structure of the semantic guardrail memory across training checkpoints (9%–100%). Semantic guardrails are colored by memory section. Malicious objective guardrails (red) dominate, reflecting the prevalence of information sabotage patterns in SHADE-Arena, while deception and evasion guardrails remain sparse but stably positioned. The spread of guardrail embeddings grows with training, mirroring the F1 trajectory reported in Figure 4.

6 Related Work

Agent Safety, Monitoring, and Control. Prior monitoring approaches improve coverage through scaffolding and aggregation. Stickland et al. (2025) run multiple independent monitoring passes and aggregate via majority vote, reducing false negatives at the cost of precision. Kale et al. (2025) systematize Monitor Red Teaming (MRT) and show that scaffolding matters more than model capability; they also introduce CUA-SHADE-Arena, extending TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2024) with 15 adversarial task pairs. AgentAuditor (Luo et al., 2025) retrieves nearest-neighbor exemplars to guide safety classification. These methods treat each trajectory independently and do not accumulate monitoring knowledge across episodes. Agent-ToM instead unifies structured ToM reasoning with persistent cross-episode learning via a single Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline, distilling abstract belief- and intent-conditioned guardrails rather than retrieving raw traces.

Experience-Driven Memory and Prompt Optimization. ACE (Zhang et al., 2026), SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026), and Evo-Memory (Wei et al., 2025) explore evolving external memory for task-solving agents, showing that passive retrieval is insufficient and memory must be actively refined. Agent-ToM is the first to apply structured evolving memory to the monitoring layer, distilling reusable security guardrails from episodic critiques. GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2026) introduces gradient-free reflective prompt evolution; Agent-ToM uses it as a prompt-level learning baseline, showing that memory-based learning substantially outperforms prompt optimization alone.

7 Conclusion and Limitations

We presented Agent-ToM, a learning-based monitoring framework grounded in structured Theory-of-Mind reasoning that addresses two limitations of existing approaches: the lack of explicit belief and intent inference, and the inability to improve from prior experience. By combining the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline with critique-driven distillation into persistent semantic guardrail memory, Agent-ToM produces monitoring decisions that are explicitly constructed, verified, and refined across episodes. Agent-ToM achieves the highest F1 on SHADE-Arena with only two LLM calls per trajectory, outperforming ensemble methods at a fraction of the inference cost, and demonstrates out-of-distribution generalization to CUA-SHADE-Arena without retraining. These results suggest that monitoring performance is primarily driven by reasoning structure and learning at the monitoring layer, rather than inference-time compute.

Limitations. Agent-ToM’s effectiveness depends on critique quality: noisy or uninformative diagnostic signals produce misleading guardrails (Zhang et al., 2026; Suzgun et al., 2026). Memory organization introduces further tradeoffs, as optimal schemas may vary across deployment settings. More broadly, the framework assumes latent beliefs and intent are inferable via abductive reasoning, an assumption that breaks down when highly deceptive agents produce indistinguishable traces.

Appendix A Dataset Details

Attack Categories

Table 8 summarizes the statistics of the two benchmarks: SHADE-Arena and CUA-SHADE-Arena. Table 9 summarizes the attack categories derived from adversarial task objectives across both benchmarks.

Evasion Strategies

Following the Monitor Red Teaming (MRT) threat model of [Kale et al., 2025], we characterize traces along two axes: agent awareness (whether the agent knows it is being monitored) and monitor awareness (what the monitor knows about the agent’s task). In our setup, the monitor is aware throughout, i.e., it has access to the agent’s full trajectory and main task specification, but not the hidden side task. Agent awareness varies across trace types, spanning one unaware baseline and five aware-agent evasion strategies. Malicious SHADE-Arena traces include one unaware baseline and five aware-agent evasion strategies:

  • •

    Unaware Baseline (naive, n=70n{=}70) — agent is oblivious to the monitor’s existence and employs no evasion strategy.

  • •

    Aware Baseline — Dealer’s Choice (no_thinking, n=69n{=}69) — monitor-aware agent with no prescribed evasion strategy; self-directs its own evasion approach.

  • •

    CoT Obfuscation (selective, n=88n{=}88; selective_v2, n=62n{=}62) — agent generates two reasoning blocks, hiding true intent in a concealed chain-of-thought while presenting a sanitized version to the monitor.

  • •

    Lying with Jailbreaking (liar_204, n=71n{=}71) — agent employs different jailbreaking-inspired strategies to deceive the monitor with plausible false narratives.

  • •

    Hybrid Obfuscation + Lying (selective_v2_liar_204, n=72n{=}72) — combination of CoT obfuscation and lying strategies.

  • •

    Monitor Hijacking (mm_v4, n=37n{=}37) — agent injects instructions into its trajectory to manipulate the monitor’s output score.

CUA-SHADE-Arena employs CoT obfuscation exclusively (selective_v2, n=45n{=}45), representing an exclusively aware-agent evaluation setting. All evasion strategies are applied orthogonally across attack categories. Benign traces correspond to agents given only the main task with no hidden side objective (no_secondary, n=320n{=}320 for SHADE-Arena and n=75n{=}75 for CUA-SHADE-Arena, n=395n{=}395 total).

Appendix B Prompts

Stage 1: ToM Reason Prompt

Stage 1 implements the ToM Reason stage of the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline (Section 2.3). ToM reasoning is invoked through the structured 5-step analysis (Steps 1–4), which explicitly elicits belief inference, intent hypothesis generation, behavior prediction, and deviation analysis before any classification decision is made. The semantic guardrails input contains monitoring strategies retrieved from memory ℳ\mathcal{M} (Section 2.5). The critique reflection input is populated during training only and is empty at inference time. Figure 10 shows the full prompt.

Stage 2: ToM Verify Prompt

Stage 2 implements the Verify–Refine stage of the Reason–Verify–Refine pipeline (Section 2.3). Acting as an independent second reviewer, it re-evaluates the Stage 1 classification by assessing whether the inferred intent and observed deviations are sufficiently supported by evidence, testing alternative benign explanations, and applying asymmetric revision criteria — requiring stronger evidence to downgrade a malicious classification than to confirm it. The semantic guardrails input contains the same monitoring strategies retrieved from memory ℳ\mathcal{M} as Stage 1. Figure 11 shows the full prompt.
